title: 4.6.2 Where each instrument acts
pars: Fifteen of the twenty-four instruments act in start-up (Figure 4.2), a phase that produces almost no participant data and in which the site decides whether the data that follow will be usable. The training and credentialing decisions, the risk register, and the readiness of imaging are completed there, and the rules of most other instruments, from the criticality grades to the indicator thresholds, are fixed before the first participant. The records of each participant, from the eligibility decision to the visit record, open only in the phase where their data arise, and the indicators and the complication review, although prepared early, say little until cases accumulate. Only the milestone reviews act in every phase, and the post-investigation debrief acts only in the closing phase.

Within start-up, the order follows what each instrument reads from another. The training requirements and the criticality grades come before anyone is released for a task, the release on device training comes before the credentialing decision that draws on it, and the plan for internal verification comes before its first review.

Four orders follow from the gaps that the framework answers, and none of the instruments compared in Chapter 3 imposes them. The risk register opens before the first participant, because a register opened later records risks that have already been taken (Gap 2). The basis of comparison of the learning curve log is fixed before the first case, so the curve of each surgeon starts with that surgeon’s first case, including a surgeon who joins during conduct (Gap 3). Internal verification has its scope and cadence set before conduct begins, in its plan or on its checklist, so it runs on the site’s own calendar, independent of the sponsor’s visits (Gap 4). The rule of each indicator in use is fixed before the first participant, which lets a signal open a corrective action before an external finding does (Gap 5).

Whether failures also concentrate in particular phases is a separate question, which the evidence answers only in part. Surgical complications may cluster in the early part of a surgeon’s learning curve [22], and loss to follow-up accumulates over the later years [24], but these findings do not show that a site that activates its controls by phase does better than one that acts when the sponsor’s monitoring asks it to. The framework therefore treats its organization by phases as a design hypothesis, consistent with ICH E8(R1), which directs quality resources toward critical activities and risks [5]. If the controls of the conduct phases work, close-out should also find less to correct, an expected benefit that this thesis has not measured.
